parts:
Hi,


I am trying to replicate the Martin, Quinn (2002) paper ( http://mqscores.berkeley.edu/media/pa02.pdf ) regarding US Supreme Court. They estimated ideal points for Justices between 1953 and 1999, employing MCMC written in C++. It is a Dynamic IRT with y_ijt = - a_i + b_i * x_jt, ‘i’ relates to cases, ‘t’ relates to terms, and ‘j’ relates to justices. Each justice has an ideal point per term and each term follows a random walk.


I have implemented the model in Stan, but it has not worked. Sampling process starts; however, I let my computer running all day long and the program stopped in the first sampling process: “SAMPLING FOR MODEL '012821a913ef3a61e1f8322e5da761ba' NOW (CHAIN 1).

Chain 1, Iteration:     1 / 100000 [  0%]  (Warmup)”



I started using Stan a couple of weeks ago, so I am not sure if I coded it right. It was not easy to prepare the data for processing in Stan, but I think I fulfilled this task. I believe it could be an issue with my model. Could someone check my Stan code (posted below)?


Thank you so much,


Duarte


The entire code: http://github.com/duarteguilherme/Quinn-martin-replication


Stan code: ‘

data {

int<lower=0> N;

int<lower=0> ncas; // number of cases

int<lower=0> njus; // number of justices

int<lower=0> npar; // number of parameters

int<lower=0> cas[N];

int<lower=0> par[N];

int<lower=0> in_ter[njus];

int<lower=0> fi_ter[njus];

int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N];

}

parameters {

real beta0[ncas];

real beta1[ncas];

vector[npar] x;

real sigma[njus];

}


model {


 for (i in 1:N){

 y[i] ~ bernoulli(Phi_approx(x[par[i]]*beta1[cas[i]] - beta0[cas[i]]));

 }

 

 

 for (i in 1:ncas) {

 beta1 ~ normal(0, 1);

 }

 for (i in 1:ncas) {

 beta0 ~ normal(0, 1);

 }

 for (j in 1:njus) {

   if ( j == 3 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(-3,.01); // Justice Douglas, term=0, set prior to normal(-3,.01)

   }

   else if ( j == 1 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(1,.01); // Justice Harlam, term=0, set prior to normal(1,.01)

   }

   else if ( j == 5 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(-2,.01); // Justice Marshall, term=0, set prior to normal(-2,.01)

   }

   else if ( j == 6 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(-2,.01); // Justice Brennan, term=0, set prior to normal(-2,.01)

   }

   else if ( j == 10 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(1,.01); // Justice Frankfurter, term=0, set prior to normal(1,.01)

   }

   else if ( j == 14 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(-1,.01); // Justice Fortas, term=0, set prior to normal(-1,.01)

   }

   else if ( j == 21 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(2,.01); // Justice Rehnquist, term=0, set prior to normal(2,.01)

   }

   else if ( j == 24 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(2.5,.01); // Justice Scalie, term=0, set prior to normal(2.5,.01)

   }

   else if ( j == 27 ) {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(2.5,.01); // Justice Thomas, term=0, set prior to normal(2.5,.01)

   }


   else {

     x[in_ter[j]] ~ normal(0,1);

   }

   if ( in_ter[j]!=fi_ter[j]) {

     for (k in (in_ter[j]+1):fi_ter[j]) {

       x[k] ~ normal(x[k-1],sigma[j]);

     }

   }

 }

 

}

'

Hi, buncha things going on here, including:
1.  Don’t plan to run 10^5 iterations.  If your model is making sense, 1000 should be a reasonable number.
2.  If you’re using normal(1, .01) priors, you’ll have to specify the init in that range.  But do you really want to be specifying normal(1, .01) priors?  I suspect it’s better to just input these numbers as data.
3.  You can vectorize your normal distribution and it will run faster.

To implement Andrew's suggestion (2), see the manual chapter
on missing data. You can think of all the unobserved justice
parameters as missing data.

You won't need to do all that if-else fiddling with priors that way,
but there'll be a more complexed transformed parameters block.

What is npar vs. njus?

Assuming x is supposed to be the parameter for the justices,
I don't see why it's indexed by npar rather than njus and
I don't see why there are njus sigma terms for the hierarchical
priors for x.

The parameterization looks like a 2PL-irt with beta1 and beta0 being
case parameters and x being the justice parameter.
> y[i] ~ bernoulli(Phi_approx(x[par[i]]*beta1[cas[i]] - beta0[cas[i]]));

It'll be more efficient with logit because we have a built-in
bernoulli_logit that takes a parameter on a logit scale. The
choice of logit vs. probit is usually a computational convenience
one as the tails are very similar --- Gelman and Hill discuss in
their regression book.

The main problem with these ideal point models is exactly what you're
trying to code around --- the lack of identifiability due to sign flips.
Trying to identify by setting particular values is challenging. Let us
know if it works. This is also discussed in the Gelman and Hill regression
book.

- Bob

I can't believe I'm pickier than Andrew on a graph, but it
makes sense given that I'm a computer scientist and read
these differently than Andrew does.

I'm OK with it as is given some strong qualification in the
caption. We have to make it clear that the caption has I + J
on the X axis, you can't recover I or J just by looking at
the axis, that the growth is expected to be proportional to
I * J, not I + J. And extra credit for pointing out that with
a fixed problem set size I, growth is linear in J if just J grows.

What worries me about this graph is that someone will look at
it as saying the growth is quadratic in the number of parameters.
That's not quite right without the assumption that the items and
people size grow at the same rate.

- Bob

Thanks. I didn't realize it had a time series inside. We're
working on IRT models a lot these days and I want to use this
one as an example of the differences with ideal-point models.

Here's what I came up with from the original paper, coded
in "long form" or "database form" or like a data frame in R.
I wasn't clear from skimming the model section of the paper what
priors were being used for alpha and beta and theta in the first
term --- I'd be inclined to make the model hierarchical.

What you'd need to do is actually set some of the theta values
by hand and let the other ones float. You do that by defining
smaller vectors of the ones that float and then constructing ones
together that don't. But hwy set all the justices in term 0? Do
you really want Scalia and Thomas to both have position 2.5 in term 0?
And by term 0 did you mean term 1 if we're numbering from 1? I got
a bit lost between yours and Martin and Quinn's notation. I tried
to stick to theirs below.


/**
* Martin and Quinn (2002) Dynamic Ideal Point Estimation via
* Markov Chain Monte Carlo for the U.S. Supreme Court, 1953--1999.
*
* Model section of paper is silent on fixed (?) priors for params.
*/
data {
int<lower=0> T; // number of terms
int<lower=0> J; // number of justices
int<lower=0> K; // total number of cases

int<lower=0> N; // num votes
int<lower=1> tt[N]; // term for vote n
int<lower=1> jj[N]; // justice for vote n
int<lower=1> kk[N]; // case for vote n
int<lower=0, upper=1> z[N]; // vote (yea = 1, nay = 0)

vector[J] theta0; // prior mean (M&Q: mu0)
vector<lower=0>[J] delta0; // initial t sd (M&Q: sqrt of C[0,])
vector<lower=0>[J] delta[T-1]; // "evolution sd" (M&Q: sqrt of Delta[t,j])
vector[2] b0; // prior mean for pos and discrim
cov_matrix[2] B0; // prior covar for pos and discrim
}
parameters {
vector[2] alpha_beta[K]; // position and discrim of case k
vector[J] theta[T]; // position in term t of justice j
}
model {
for (n in 1:N)
z[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha_beta[kk[n], 1]
+ alpha_beta[kk[n], 2] * theta[tt[n], jj[n]]);

alpha_beta ~ multi_normal(b0, B0);

theta[1] ~ normal(theta0, delta0);
for (t in 2:T)
theta[t] ~ normal(theta[t - 1], delta[t - 1]);
}


If you get this working, can you send it back to us? Or even better,
write it up in knitr as a case study? We're about to start publishing
them on our web site for example models. Sort of like the BUGS examples,
only new ones with a bit more description.

- Bob

 *  Martin and Quinn (2002) Dynamic Ideal Point Estimation via
 *  Markov Chain Monte Carlo for the U.S. Supreme Court, 1953--1999.
 *
 *  Model section of paper is silent on fixed (?) priors for params.
 */
data {
  int<lower=0> T;                 // number of terms
  int<lower=0> J;                 // number of justices
  int<lower=0> K;                 // total number of cases

  int<lower=0> N;                 // num votes
  int<lower=1> tt[N];             // term for vote n
  int<lower=1> jj[N];             // justice for vote n
  int<lower=1> kk[N];             // case for vote n
  int<lower=0, upper=1> z[N];     // vote (yea = 1, nay = 0)

  vector[J] theta0;               // prior mean (M&Q: mu0)
  vector<lower=0>[J] delta0;      // initial t sd (M&Q: sqrt of C[0,])
  vector<lower=0>[J] delta[T-1];  // "evolution sd"  (M&Q: sqrt of Delta[t,j])
  vector[2] b0;                   // prior mean for pos and discrim
  cov_matrix[2] B0;               // prior covar for pos and discrim
}
parameters {
  vector[2] alpha_beta[K];        // position and discrim of case k
  vector[J] theta[T];             // position in term t of justice j
}
model {
  for (n in 1:N)
    z[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha_beta[kk[n], 1]
                           + alpha_beta[kk[n], 2] * theta[tt[n], jj[n]]);

  alpha_beta ~ multi_normal(b0, B0);

  theta[1] ~ normal(theta0, delta0);
  for (t in 2:T)
    theta[t] ~ normal(theta[t - 1], delta[t - 1]);
}

write it up in knitr as a case study?  We're about to start publishing
them on our web site for example models.  Sort of like the BUGS examples,
only new ones with a bit more description.

- Bob
